newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans rally ranks for budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans rally ranks for budget deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican leaders rallied their ranks on Tuesday for expected passage later this week of a historic accord to balance the budget and give the first major tax cuts in 16 years.

White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles said he expected a majority of Democrats would vote for the package which he and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin presented to House Democrats at a closed meeting.
Republican leaders also expected most of their members would vote for both the spending bill and the tax cuts.

Clinton was to appear with Democratic leaders at the White House on Tuesday afternoon to praise the merits of the deal which will give a $500 per child tax credit, set up a $24 billion children's health insurance programme and cut tax rates paid by investors.

"There is an overwhelming sentiment in our group of a major success for the president and our party," Democratic conference chairman Vic Fazio of California told reporters after the meeting with White House officials.
"The president got basically everything he wanted out of this deal," New York Democrat Gary Ackerman said.
The sentiment was largely the same in the Senate where Minority Leader Tom Daschle told reporters: "An overwhelming majority of Democrats will support this agreement."

Democrats were largely left out of the negotiations between the White House and Republicans who control Congress. House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt's office said he would not be attending the ceremony at the White House.

Several Democrats said they feared the plan would squeeze domestic spending in the fourth and fifth year as it allowed only a 0.5 percent average annual increase, an amount below the expected rate of inflation.

Massachusetts Democrat Barney Frank warned that it would make the federal tax system less fair and would crimp education, environmental and transportion budgets. "For housing, it's an eviction budget," he said adding it would result in fewer federally subsidised houses and apartments.
But these reservations were not widely shared. Ackerman said many lawmakers from his state welcomed the cut in the capital gains tax rate.

Sen. Phil Gramm of Texas, who had held out for larger tax cuts, said he was now inclined to support that portion of the bill as the total was now around $90 billion in net tax cuts over five years. But he added he might not vote for the spending cut bill due to its Medicare provisions. "We are not doing enough to reform Medicare," he told reporters.
Clinton sought and received assurances that three issues had been taken care of: spending for education, a child tax credit, and an expansion of health benefits for poor children.

Republicans also won provisions including a cut in the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent, down from the current 28 percent, and a second drop to 18 percent in 2001 for long-term holdings. Estate taxes were also eased.

The $500-per-child tax credit was extended as Clinton wanted to those who earn as little as $18,000 a year and boosted on the other side to cover most of the middle class with a phase-out starting at $110,000 as Republicans sought. This tax credit will be worth $85 billion over five years.

To bring the budget to balance, the plan slows the rate of growth in many federal social programmes and reduces Medicare costs by $115 billion over five years. At the last minute lawmakers and the White House backed off a plan to require wealthier senior citizens to pay higher Medicare premiums.
The plan will raise the 24 cent-per-pack cigarette tax by 15 cents and will extend the airline ticket tax to raise about $33 billion through 2002.

Clinton won a new $24 billion programme to provide health insurance to cover up to 2.2 million uninsured children. They also accepted his education proposals including $31 billion in Hope scholarships for post-secondary studies.
